data.title: Supplier Relationships Are Publicly Mapped
data.summary: Case studies, press releases, procurement records and shared job postings identified the organisation's suppliers and the systems they support, which is the information an invoice-fraud or supply-chain pretext is built from.
data.description:
Suppliers are published for good reasons — case studies, certifications, public tenders — and the result is a map of who may legitimately contact the organisation, about what, and with what access.

Invoice fraud follows directly: a message from a near-miss of the supplier's domain, referencing the real project, asking to update bank details. Nothing about it is implausible, because the relationship is real.

The same map supports access pretexts. A caller claiming to be from the named managed service provider, during an upgrade window announced in a case study, is asking for something the organisation is expecting.
data.recommendation:
* Treat the detailed supplier list as sensitive; publish case studies without naming the systems involved.
* Require out-of-band verification for any change to payment details, through a contact of record and never a number from the request.
* Tell suppliers how you will contact them and how to verify you, so the verification runs both ways.
* Monitor for look-alike domains of significant suppliers, not only your own.
data.short_recommendation: Treat the supplier list as sensitive and verify payment changes out of band.
